meta.title: Cerebellum Atlas
meta.subtitle: An evidence-linked map of the cerebellum, from molecules to mind
meta.disclaimer: Summaries, link statuses and map scores were drafted with AI assistance from PubMed abstracts and need review by domain experts. Diagrams are schematic.

statuses.label: Established
statuses.desc: Replicated across labs and methods; textbook level.

statuses.label: Supported
statuses.desc: Several consistent studies; details still open.

statuses.label: Emerging
statuses.desc: One or a few studies, or a single method or species.

statuses.label: Hypothesis
statuses.desc: Proposed and plausible, not directly tested.

statuses.label: Gap
statuses.desc: No curated link: a candidate for new research.

evidence.label: Causal manipulation
evidence.desc: Lesion, genetic, opto-/chemogenetic, pharmacological or stimulation experiments.

evidence.label: Patients & lesions
evidence.desc: Patient cohorts, lesion–symptom mapping, human genetics.

evidence.label: Recording & imaging
evidence.desc: Electrophysiology, calcium imaging, fMRI without manipulation.

manipulate: Cell-type-specific knockout or knock-in (e.g., Pcp2/L7-Cre for Purkinje cells)
Inducible or acute protein inactivation (avoids developmental compensation)
In vivo CRISPR or viral gene knockdown
readout: Immunostaining of zebrin and PLCβ stripes

manipulate: Opto-/chemogenetics of a defined cell type
Slice plasticity protocols (PF alone vs. PF + CF pairing)
readout: Two-photon calcium or voltage imaging of dendrites

manipulate: Closed-loop climbing-fiber stimulation timed to behavior
readout: Neuropixels recording across cortex and nuclei

manipulate: Pathway-specific inhibition of a relay (e.g., thalamic nucleus)
Task designs that dissociate prediction, timing and reward

manipulate: Drug repurposing in genetic models (e.g., mTOR inhibitors)

entities.name: mGluR1
entities.summary: Metabotropic glutamate receptor on Purkinje-cell spines, recruited by strong parallel-fiber activity. It drives PLCβ, PKC and calcium signaling needed to induce LTD. Knockout mice lack LTD and have impaired eyeblink conditioning, but they are also ataxic.

entities.name: Protein kinase C
entities.summary: Kinase downstream of mGluR1 whose activity triggers AMPA-receptor internalization during LTD. Blocking it in Purkinje cells (L7-PKCI mice) disrupts PF–PC plasticity and impairs hippocampal place coding that relies on self-motion cues.

entities.name: AMPA receptors (GluA2)
entities.summary: Mediate fast parallel fiber–Purkinje transmission. LTD is expressed as clathrin-dependent endocytosis of GluA2-containing receptors. Mice that cannot internalize them lack LTD yet learn normally.

entities.name: PLCβ3 / PLCβ4
entities.summary: Phospholipase C isoforms downstream of mGluR1, expressed in complementary stripes: PLCβ3 in zebrin-positive and PLCβ4 in zebrin-negative Purkinje cells. The same receptor therefore engages different signaling machinery in different modules.

entities.name: TRPC3 channel
entities.summary: Cation channel activated downstream of mGluR1. Blocking it reduces the higher simple-spike rate of zebrin-negative Purkinje cells, so modules operate at different intrinsic frequencies.

entities.name: GluD2–Cbln1 complex
entities.summary: Cbln1 secreted by granule cells binds the orphan receptor GluD2 on Purkinje spines. The complex organizes parallel fiber–Purkinje synapses from both sides and can induce new synapses.

entities.name: Zebrin II (aldolase C)
entities.summary: Expressed by subsets of Purkinje cells in parasagittal stripes conserved across vertebrates. Zebrin-positive and zebrin-negative modules differ in firing rate, signaling and plasticity.

entities.name: CACNA1A (Cav2.1)
entities.summary: α1A subunit of the P/Q-type calcium channel, abundant in Purkinje cells. Small polyglutamine expansions cause spinocerebellar ataxia type 6.

entities.name: ATXN1
entities.summary: Gene with an unstable CAG repeat. Expansion causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 1, and longer repeats are associated with earlier onset.

entities.name: TSC1 / mTOR pathway
entities.summary: Losing Tsc1 in Purkinje cells lowers their excitability and causes autistic-like behaviors in mice, which rapamycin prevents. PC-Tsc1 mice became a test bed for mapping cerebellar circuits relevant to autism.

entities.name: SHANK2
entities.summary: Postsynaptic scaffold gene linked to autism. Its loss impairs Purkinje intrinsic plasticity and PF–PC LTP, enhances inhibition and makes simple spikes irregular. Purkinje-specific knockouts show motor-learning and social deficits.

entities.name: FMR1 (FMRP)
entities.summary: Fragile X gene. Deleting it in Purkinje cells enhances LTD, elongates spines and impairs eyeblink conditioning, resembling the deficits of fragile X patients.

entities.name: Dopamine D1 receptor
entities.summary: Marks a distinct, mostly GABAergic population in the lateral cerebellar nucleus (also present in human dentate). Inhibiting these neurons impairs working memory, response inhibition, spatial memory and prepulse inhibition.

entities.name: Atoh1 (Math1)
entities.summary: Transcription factor of the rhombic lip. Required for generating granule neurons.

entities.name: Ptf1a
entities.summary: Transcription factor of the cerebellar ventricular zone that specifies GABAergic neurons: Purkinje cells and interneurons.

entities.name: Sonic hedgehog
entities.summary: Secreted by Purkinje cells; drives proliferation of granule-cell precursors. Over-activation of the pathway underlies SHH-type medulloblastoma.

entities.name: SCN2A (NaV1.2)
entities.summary: Autism-risk sodium-channel gene. In granule cells, NaV1.2 supports high-frequency transmission and LTP at parallel fiber–Purkinje synapses. Its loss leaves the VOR hypersensitive in mice and children, and restoring expression rescues VOR plasticity.

entities.name: ZP2 (human granule cells)
entities.summary: A sperm-receptor gene co-opted in human granule cells. Pontine mossy fibers induce it, and it reduces synaptic proteins at mossy fiber–granule glomeruli and dampens activity: a human-specific synaptic regulator.

entities.name: Purkinje cell
entities.summary: The sole output neuron of the cerebellar cortex (GABAergic). Each receives more than 100,000 parallel-fiber synapses but usually a single climbing fiber (some multi-dendritic cells keep more), and fires simple spikes and complex spikes. Population simple-spike activity predicts movement kinematics. Molecular identity (zebrin) varies by module.

entities.name: Granule cell
entities.summary: The most numerous neurons in the brain (~60 billion in humans). Each receives about four mossy-fiber inputs, which theory says maximizes coding dimension. Population activity is high-dimensional but often denser than classic theory assumed, and it carries predictive, reward-expectation and seconds-long timing signals.

entities.name: Golgi cell
entities.summary: Inhibitory interneuron of the granular layer that provides feedforward and feedback inhibition to granule cells, shaping the timing and sparseness of the input layer.

entities.name: Molecular-layer interneurons
entities.summary: Stellate and basket cells, now split into two molecularly distinct types (MLI1, MLI2). They inhibit Purkinje cells and grade climbing-fiber calcium signals, which can flip the sign of plasticity and learning.

entities.name: Unipolar brush cell
entities.summary: Glutamatergic interneuron concentrated in vestibular lobules that amplifies and prolongs single mossy-fiber inputs. Gene expression varies continuously rather than in discrete types.

entities.name: Cerebellar nuclear neurons
entities.summary: Excitatory projection neurons plus inhibitory (including olive-projecting) neurons. Each nucleus repeats a conserved set of two excitatory and three inhibitory classes; the fastigial nucleus has five output-specific excitatory classes.

entities.name: Inferior olive neurons
entities.summary: Electrically coupled neurons with subthreshold oscillations that give rise to climbing fibers. Their activity is sculpted by GABAergic feedback from the cerebellar nuclei.

entities.name: PF–Purkinje LTD
entities.summary: Depression of parallel fiber–Purkinje synapses after conjunctive PF and CF activity (high calcium). Predicted by Albus and demonstrated by Ito. It needs mGluR1/PKC signaling and AMPA-receptor endocytosis. Whether it is necessary for learning is debated.

entities.name: PF–Purkinje LTP & intrinsic plasticity
entities.summary: Potentiation induced by parallel-fiber activity without a climbing-fiber signal (lower calcium), the counterpart of LTD in an inverse BCM rule. Intrinsic excitability also changes. Both are lost in Shank2 mutants.

entities.name: Rhombic lip & ventricular zone
entities.summary: Two germinal zones: the Atoh1-positive rhombic lip makes glutamatergic neurons (granule cells, unipolar brush cells, nuclear projection neurons) and the Ptf1a-positive ventricular zone makes GABAergic neurons. In humans the rhombic lip is uniquely expanded and long-lived.

entities.name: Mossy fiber → granule → parallel fiber
entities.summary: The main input stream. Mossy fibers from pontine, spinal, vestibular and reticular nuclei excite granule cells, whose parallel fibers run along the folium and contact many Purkinje cells.

entities.name: Climbing fiber pathway
entities.summary: One climbing fiber from the inferior olive per Purkinje cell, producing complex spikes. Classically viewed as a motor-error teaching signal, it also carries reward, reward-prediction and learned predictive signals.

entities.name: Expansion recoding
entities.summary: Marr–Albus idea that the vast granule layer recodes mossy-fiber patterns into high-dimensional, separable codes for Purkinje-cell learning. The few inputs per granule cell maximize coding dimension in theory, granule-cell axon populations are high-dimensional, and Golgi inhibition decorrelates them. How sparse the code is remains debated.

entities.name: Feedforward inhibition
entities.summary: Parallel fibers excite molecular-layer interneurons that then inhibit Purkinje cells, sharpening timing and gating climbing-fiber calcium. Purkinje-cell collaterals add feedback within zones.

entities.name: Microzones & modules
entities.summary: Strips of Purkinje cells that share climbing-fiber input from one olive subregion and project to one nuclear group. This olivo-cortico-nuclear module is the putative unit of computation.

entities.name: Zebrin± modules (upbound / downbound)
entities.summary: Zebrin-negative modules fire faster and are proposed to learn mainly by increasing activity ('upbound'); zebrin-positive modules fire slower and learn by decreasing it ('downbound').

entities.name: Internal (forward) models
entities.summary: Theory that cerebellar circuits learn to predict the sensory consequences of commands (forward models) or to generate commands (inverse models). The idea has been extended to thought and to social prediction.

entities.name: Reward & prediction signals
entities.summary: Climbing fibers and granule cells carry reward expectation, delivery and omission signals in specific microzones, in mice and monkeys. Granule cells can ramp toward a reward over seconds. This suggests cerebellar learning also uses reinforcement-like teaching signals.

entities.name: Distributed synergistic plasticity
entities.summary: Learning spread across many plasticity sites (PF–PC LTD and LTP, interneuron synapses, intrinsic excitability, cerebellar and vestibular nuclei) that act together. This can explain learning when one mechanism is removed.

entities.name: Crus I / vermis → thalamus → mPFC circuit
entities.summary: Right Crus I and posterior vermis connect through the cerebellar nuclei and ventromedial thalamus to medial prefrontal cortex. In mice these circuits regulate social and flexible behavior, and they are disrupted in autism models.

entities.name: Anterior lobe (I–V)
entities.summary: Primary sensorimotor cerebellum with an inverted somatotopic body map. Lesions here cause ataxia rather than cognitive deficits.

entities.name: Lobule VI
entities.summary: Transition zone: hand and face sensorimotor representation plus language, spatial and executive activations. In mice, juvenile perturbation of lobule VI alters reversal learning.

entities.name: Crus I
entities.summary: Large association territory coupled to frontoparietal and default-mode networks. Right Crus I is engaged in language and mentalizing, and its dysfunction is implicated in autism.

entities.name: Crus II
entities.summary: Association territory in a closed loop with prefrontal area 46 in monkeys. In humans it is active in mentalizing, executive and language tasks.

entities.name: Lobule VIIB
entities.summary: Linked with executive and working-memory activations and frontoparietal control networks.

entities.name: Lobule VIII
entities.summary: Second, upright sensorimotor map; also attention networks. Right lobule VIII lesions are associated with spatial deficits.

entities.name: Lobule IX
entities.summary: Hemispheric IX joins the third nonmotor (default-mode) representation; vermal IX (uvula) contributes to oculomotor and vestibular control.

entities.name: Lobule X & flocculus
entities.summary: Vestibulo-cerebellum for gaze and balance, with direct projections to the vestibular nuclei. The flocculus is the classic site of VOR-adaptation studies.

entities.name: Posterior vermis (VI–IX)
entities.summary: Midline posterior lobe: oculomotor control (VI–VII) and affective and autonomic functions. Vermis injury is associated with affective symptoms and with worse outcomes after preterm cerebellar injury.

entities.name: Vermis (midline zone)
entities.summary: Midline cortex projecting to the fastigial nucleus: axial posture, gait and eye movements, plus autonomic and affective functions.

entities.name: Paravermis (intermediate zone)
entities.summary: Intermediate cortex projecting to the interposed nuclei: limb control and associative motor learning such as eyeblink conditioning.

entities.name: Lateral hemispheres
entities.summary: Lateral cortex projecting to the dentate nucleus. It supports movement planning and sequencing and, through loops with association cortex, cognitive, language and social functions. Expanded in apes and especially humans.

entities.name: Fastigial nucleus
entities.summary: Medial nucleus and output of the vermis. Five glutamatergic classes target posturomotor, oromotor, autonomic, orienting and vigilance circuits. Outputs to thalamus and PAG support motor planning and fear memory.

entities.name: Interposed nucleus
entities.summary: Output of the paravermis to the red nucleus and thalamus. Essential for conditioned eyeblink responses.

entities.name: Dentate (lateral) nucleus
entities.summary: Output of the lateral hemispheres. It projects via thalamus to motor and prefrontal cortex (area 46) and to striatum. Greatly expanded in humans, where a frontal-projecting excitatory class predominates.

entities.name: Cerebellar cortex
entities.summary: A tightly folded sheet with ~78% of the neocortex's surface area in humans and most of the brain's neurons. The same three-layer microcircuit repeats across functionally distinct modules.

entities.name: Deep cerebellar nuclei
entities.summary: The main output of the cerebellum (fastigial, interposed, dentate). Targets include thalamus, brainstem motor nuclei, VTA, PAG and inferior olive. The nuclei evolved by duplicating a conserved cell-type set.

entities.name: Vestibular nuclei
entities.summary: Brainstem nuclei that receive direct Purkinje input from the vestibulo-cerebellum. They drive the VOR and are a site of motor memory.

entities.name: Pontine nuclei
entities.summary: Relay from much of the neocortex to the cerebellar cortex as mossy fibers, mostly to the opposite side. Also relays subthalamic input to the cerebellum.

entities.name: Inferior olive
entities.summary: Sole source of climbing fibers, which cross to the opposite cerebellum. Inhibitory feedback from the cerebellar nuclei closes the olivo-cortico-nuclear loop.

entities.name: Thalamus
entities.summary: Relays cerebellar output to cortex: motor thalamus to motor and prefrontal areas, ventromedial thalamus to mPFC, intralaminar nuclei to striatum, and parafascicular nucleus in anxiety.

entities.name: Motor & premotor cortex
entities.summary: Forms closed loops with the cerebellum (cortico-pontine input; nuclear output via thalamus). In mice, a frontal–fastigial loop maintains motor-planning activity.

entities.name: Prefrontal cortex
entities.summary: Dorsolateral PFC (area 46), medial PFC and orbitofrontal cortex receive cerebellar output via thalamus. Cerebellar–prefrontal loops are implicated in working memory, flexibility, social behavior and schizophrenia symptoms.

entities.name: Posterior parietal cortex
entities.summary: Association cortex in loops with the cerebellum. Connectivity between right Crus I and inferior parietal lobule is altered in autism.

entities.name: Striatum
entities.summary: Receives disynaptic cerebellar input via intralaminar thalamus. This short-latency path can shape corticostriatal plasticity and, when aberrant, causes dystonia. Cerebellar nuclei also raise striatal dopamine during satiation.

entities.name: Subthalamic nucleus
entities.summary: Basal ganglia nucleus that projects disynaptically, via the pontine nuclei, to the cerebellar cortex.

entities.name: VTA (dopamine)
entities.summary: Receives monosynaptic excitatory input from the cerebellar nuclei. Activating this input is rewarding, and it is required for social preference in mice.

entities.name: Periaqueductal gray
entities.summary: Ventrolateral PAG receives fastigial input that bidirectionally controls fear-memory strength and modulates extinction.

entities.name: Hippocampus
entities.summary: Receives multisynaptic input from restricted cerebellar regions and synchronizes with them at 6–12 Hz. Cerebellar plasticity shapes place cells that rely on self-motion cues.

entities.name: Amygdala
entities.summary: Core of the fear network. A fastigial → parafascicular thalamus pathway may relay cerebellar influence to the amygdala to modulate anxiety.

entities.name: Red nucleus & brainstem motor nuclei
entities.summary: Targets of interposed and fastigial outputs (rubrospinal, reticulospinal and vestibulospinal systems) for limb and axial control.

entities.name: Spinal cord
entities.summary: Spinocerebellar pathways carry limb and trunk proprioception as mossy fibers; descending brainstem pathways carry cerebellar influence to motor neurons.

entities.name: Body (muscles & proprioceptors)
entities.summary: Movement and proprioceptive feedback. Body maps appear twice in the cerebellum (anterior lobe and lobule VIII).

entities.name: Vestibular labyrinth
entities.summary: Head-motion signals reach the vestibular nuclei and, as primary vestibular mossy fibers, the flocculonodular lobe directly.

entities.name: Eyes & visual input
entities.summary: Image motion on the retina (retinal slip) reaches the flocculus through the inferior olive as an error signal; the oculomotor vermis controls saccades.

entities.name: Gut nutrient signals
entities.summary: Nutrients infused into the gut activate anterior deep cerebellar nuclei neurons in mice. The afferent route is not yet known.

entities.name: Closed cerebro-cerebellar loops
entities.summary: Cortical areas that send input to a cerebellar region receive output from the same region. Parallel motor, prefrontal and parietal loops are the anatomical basis for nonmotor functions.

entities.name: Cerebellum–basal ganglia network
entities.summary: Disynaptic links in both directions (dentate → thalamus → striatum; subthalamic nucleus → pons → cerebellar cortex) make the two subcortical systems one network.

entities.name: Developmental sensitive periods
entities.summary: The cerebellum may instruct maturation of remote cortical circuits during sensitive periods ('developmental diaschisis'). Early disruption could then produce lasting nonmotor deficits such as autism.

entities.name: Evolutionary expansion
entities.summary: The cerebellum expanded faster than predicted in apes, and its neuron numbers scale with the neocortex's across mammals. Human Crus I/II and the frontal-projecting dentate class are enlarged, and the human cerebellar surface is ~78% of the neocortex's. Human-specific changes appear in Purkinje subtypes, granule-cell synapse genes (ZP2) and progenitor gene regulation.

entities.name: Substantia nigra pars compacta
entities.summary: Dopamine neurons that project to the dorsal striatum. Cerebellar nuclei excite them monosynaptically, raising striatal dopamine; the input is active before movement and for reward.

entities.name: Motor coordination
entities.summary: Coordination, posture, balance and eye movements. Body maps lie in the anterior lobe and lobule VIII.

entities.name: Motor learning & adaptation
entities.summary: VOR adaptation, eyeblink conditioning, prism adaptation and locomotor learning: the classic cerebellum-dependent forms of learning.

entities.name: Timing & prediction
entities.summary: Sub-second timing of movement and perception, and predictive signals about upcoming events.

entities.name: Executive function & working memory
entities.summary: Planning, set-shifting, working memory and response inhibition; impaired after posterior cerebellar lesions.

entities.name: Language
entities.summary: Verbal fluency, grammar, reading and verbal working memory, lateralized to the right cerebellum (crossed connections with left-hemisphere language cortex).

entities.name: Social cognition
entities.summary: Mentalizing and social preference. Human imaging points to Crus I/II; mouse circuit studies implicate Crus I, vermis, VTA and mPFC pathways.

entities.name: Emotion & fear
entities.summary: Emotion perception and regulation, fear learning and extinction, and anxiety.

entities.name: Reward & motivation
entities.summary: Reward expectation and reinforcement. The cerebellum both carries reward signals and drives dopamine circuits.

entities.name: Feeding & drinking
entities.summary: Meal termination and thirst. Anterior deep-nuclei neurons reduce meal size through striatal dopamine, and Purkinje cells activated by the hormone asprosin increase water intake.

entities.name: Spatial navigation
entities.summary: Path integration and spatial memory, through interactions with the hippocampus.

entities.name: Cerebellar motor syndrome
entities.summary: Ataxia of gait and limbs, dysmetria and dysarthria, mainly after anterior-lobe (III–VI) damage.

entities.name: Cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome
entities.summary: Executive, linguistic, visuospatial and affective impairments after posterior-lobe and vermis damage, screened with the CCAS scale.

entities.name: Autism spectrum disorder
entities.summary: Perinatal cerebellar injury raises autism risk, and Purkinje-specific loss of ASD genes (Tsc1, Shank2) causes autism-like behavior in mice. Eyeblink conditioning is altered across autism mouse models. Crus I–prefrontal/parietal circuits are implicated.

entities.name: Schizophrenia
entities.summary: Framed as 'cognitive dysmetria'. Cerebellar grey matter is smaller in patients, already in the youngest. Cerebellum–DLPFC connectivity tracks negative symptoms, and TMS that restores it reduces them.

entities.name: Spinocerebellar ataxias
entities.summary: Inherited ataxias, many caused by CAG/polyglutamine expansions (SCA1: ATXN1; SCA6: CACNA1A) that affect Purkinje cells.

entities.name: Fragile X syndrome
entities.summary: FMR1 loss. Patients and Purkinje-specific knockout mice show impaired eyeblink conditioning.

entities.name: Dystonia
entities.summary: In mice, aberrant cerebellar output causes dystonia: torsinA knockdown in the adult cerebellum (not the basal ganglia) and activation of glutamatergic nuclear neurons both suffice, and the signal can reach the striatum. In humans the cerebellum contributes, but whether it is the primary site is unresolved.

entities.name: Preterm cerebellar injury
entities.summary: Cerebellar hemorrhage in preterm infants is followed by high rates of motor, language, cognitive and autism-screen problems. Even without injury, prematurity displaces cerebellar maturation, with incomplete granule-cell maturation and Purkinje refinement.

entities.name: Hyperphagia (Prader–Willi syndrome)
entities.summary: Insatiable appetite; altered cerebellar food responses in patients led to the discovery of a cerebellar satiation circuit.

entities.name: Dandy–Walker malformation
entities.summary: Malformation with posterior vermis hypoplasia, associated with disrupted development of the human rhombic lip. Exome sequencing finds a genetic cause in a minority of families and implicates vascular development.

entities.name: Medulloblastoma
entities.summary: The most common malignant childhood brain tumor. The SHH group arises from granule-cell precursors with over-active Sonic hedgehog signaling; Groups 3 and 4 trace to rhombic-lip progenitors of the unipolar-brush-cell lineage, stalled in development.

entities.name: Essential tremor
entities.summary: The most common tremor disorder. Postmortem cerebellum shows Purkinje-cell degeneration and climbing-fiber rewiring. In mice, surplus climbing-fiber synapses left by a pruning deficit drive tremor-generating cerebellar oscillations.

entities.name: General psychopathology (p factor)
entities.summary: A liability shared across common mental disorders. Higher p-factor scores go with lower pontine white-matter integrity and a smaller left lobule VIIb.

entities.name: Cognitive aging & Alzheimer's disease
entities.summary: Cerebellar regions age at different rates. Larger cerebellar volume predicts better cognition in later life and, in Alzheimer's disease, while amyloid burden is low, suggesting a reserve role.

chains.name: Cerebro-cerebellar loop
chains.desc: Prefrontal cortex → pontine nuclei → cerebellar cortex → nuclei → thalamus → prefrontal cortex: the closed loop behind nonmotor cerebellar functions.

chains.name: Climbing fibers teach motor learning
chains.desc: The classic Marr–Albus–Ito chain. The final step (LTD is necessary for learning) is debated.

chains.name: Autism gene → Purkinje → mPFC circuit
chains.desc: Purkinje-cell Tsc1 loss and Crus I → nuclei → VM thalamus → mPFC circuits regulate social behavior in mice.

chains.name: Reward signals → VTA → social behavior
chains.desc: Climbing fibers signal reward; the nuclei excite VTA. Whether cerebellar reward signals shape this output is untested.

chains.name: Vermis → fastigial → PAG fear circuit
chains.desc: Fastigial neurons projecting to ventrolateral PAG control the strength of fear memories.

chains.name: Cerebellar plasticity shapes place cells
chains.desc: PKC-dependent Purkinje-cell plasticity is needed for hippocampal place coding from self-motion cues; the pathway between them is not mapped.

chains.name: Gut → anterior DCN → striatal dopamine → satiation
chains.desc: Discovered by reverse translation from Prader–Willi syndrome; both the afferent route and the route to striatal dopamine are unknown.

chains.name: Cerebellum–DLPFC network in schizophrenia
chains.desc: Cerebellum–right DLPFC connectivity tracks negative symptoms; TMS that restores it reduces them.

chains.name: Dentate → striatum in dystonia
chains.desc: A short-latency dentate → thalamus → striatum path relays aberrant cerebellar activity that causes dystonia in mice.

chains.name: D1R+ nuclear neurons and executive function
chains.desc: A dopamine-receptive population in the lateral nucleus supports working memory and response inhibition.

chains.name: Essential tremor: unpruned climbing fibers
chains.desc: Too little GluD2 leaves surplus climbing fibers unpruned. The extra climbing fiber–Purkinje synapses drive cerebellar oscillations that generate tremor (mice and patient tissue).

chains.name: Cerebellum → substantia nigra → striatal dopamine
chains.desc: Cerebellar nuclei excite nigral dopamine neurons monosynaptically, raising striatal dopamine and locomotion. The pathway is active before movement and for reward.

chains.name: Exercise → dentate → amygdala → less anxiety
chains.desc: Rotarod exercise engages glutamatergic dentate neurons that drive PKCδ+ amygdala neurons and reduce anxiety (mouse).

chains.name: SCN2A → granule-cell LTP → VOR learning
chains.desc: Losing NaV1.2 in granule cells weakens high-frequency transmission and LTP, so VOR gain cannot be turned down. Seen in mice and children with SCN2A variants, and rescued by restoring expression.

chains.name: Rhombic-lip origins of medulloblastoma
chains.desc: Glutamatergic lineages of the human rhombic lip, expanded in our species, give rise to Group 3 and 4 medulloblastoma when progenitors stall in development.

chains.name: Climbing-fiber disinhibition gates learning
chains.desc: Synchronous climbing fibers excite MLI2 interneurons, which silence MLI1s and disinhibit Purkinje dendrites. The larger calcium signal permits LTD and learning.

questions.title: One computation or many?
questions.text: Is the same computation applied to different inputs across the cerebellar cortex ('universal transform'), or do zebrin modules, cell-type gradients and nuclear classes implement different computations?
approaches: Compare plasticity rules and Purkinje-cell dynamics between anterior motor and posterior association lobules with identical protocols.
Test whether one model class (e.g., forward model) fits responses across a multi-domain fMRI battery.
Relate posterior Purkinje-cell subtypes to their projection targets.

questions.title: What do climbing fibers teach outside the motor domain?
questions.text: Climbing fibers signal reward, reward omission and learned predictions. Do these signals drive plasticity that changes social or reward-guided behavior?
approaches: Image climbing fibers during social and reward tasks.
Closed-loop olive stimulation or suppression timed to reward prediction errors.
Test whether reward-related microzones project to VTA-targeting nuclear neurons.

questions.title: How necessary is LTD for learning?
questions.text: Mice lacking LTD expression learn normally. Is this compensation by other plasticity sites, module-specific learning rules, or evidence that LTD is not the main memory mechanism?
approaches: Acute, inducible LTD block in adults to avoid developmental compensation.
Separate manipulations of zebrin-positive and zebrin-negative modules.
Measure which plasticity sites change first during learning.

questions.title: Does the cerebellum instruct cortical development?
questions.text: Juvenile perturbation of posterior cerebellum has lasting nonmotor effects. Through which circuits does early cerebellar activity shape prefrontal maturation?
approaches: Time-limited juvenile perturbation with longitudinal prefrontal recordings.
Preterm cohorts with cerebellar injury followed with longitudinal connectivity imaging.
Rescue experiments that restore activity in the relay (VM thalamus) during the sensitive period.

questions.title: Which nuclear cell types carry nonmotor signals?
questions.text: Fastigial and dentate neurons fall into output-specific classes. Which classes carry signals for fear, reward, feeding and cognition, and are they the same across species?
approaches: Class-specific manipulation with intersectional genetics.
Projection-tagged recording during nonmotor tasks.
Cross-species comparison of human dentate classes.

questions.title: How do cerebellum and basal ganglia cooperate?
questions.text: Disynaptic links connect the two systems in both directions. What computation does the network perform during learning, and how does it fail in dystonia and Parkinson's disease?
approaches: Simultaneous recording of nuclei and striatum during learning.
Silence the intralaminar thalamic relay at defined learning stages.
Patient imaging of cerebello-striatal connectivity.

questions.title: What is special about the human cerebellum?
questions.text: Human Crus I/II, the frontal-projecting dentate class and the rhombic lip are all expanded. Which of these differences matter for human cognition and disease?
approaches: Comparative single-cell atlases across primates.
Organoid or xenograft models of the human rhombic lip.
Relate individual differences in Crus I/II size to cognition.

questions.title: Can cerebellar stimulation treat nonmotor disorders?
questions.text: Cerebellar TMS restored connectivity and reduced negative symptoms; Crus I stimulation rescued social deficits in mice. Can cerebellar neuromodulation become a targeted therapy?
approaches: Sham-controlled trials with connectivity-defined targets.
Animal models that map which cells TMS-like stimulation recruits.
Biomarkers that predict responders.

questions.title: How does gut information reach the cerebellar nuclei?
questions.text: Gut nutrients activate anterior DCN neurons that end meals through striatal dopamine. The route in is unknown; the route out could be the direct nuclear projection to substantia nigra dopamine neurons or a thalamic relay.
approaches: Trans-synaptic tracing from satiation-related anterior DCN neurons.
Vagal or spinal afferent manipulation during nutrient infusion.
Test whether the dopamine effect requires VTA/SNc or a thalamic relay.

questions.title: Do functional boundaries follow anatomical modules?
questions.text: Task-based parcellations do not follow lobular boundaries. Do they follow zebrin modules, climbing-fiber zones or cerebral connectivity instead?
approaches: High-resolution fMRI compared with zebrin maps in primates.
Individual-level parcellations in dense-sampling datasets.
Map climbing-fiber zones in tasks that span domains.

questions.title: Two dopamine routes?
questions.text: Cerebellar nuclei excite both VTA and substantia nigra dopamine neurons. Do the two routes carry different signals (reward versus movement vigor), and does either carry the satiation signal from the anterior nuclei?
approaches: Record cerebellar axons in VTA and SNc in one task with reward, movement and satiety epochs.
Silence each route during feeding and during reward learning while measuring striatal dopamine with sensors.
Map which nuclear output classes project to each target.

questions.title: When does a climbing fiber teach?
questions.text: Climbing fibers fire all the time, yet learning needs strong Purkinje calcium. Synchrony recruits MLI2 disinhibition. Is synchrony the gate, and what sets it: olivary coupling, error salience or reward?
approaches: Change olivary gap-junction coupling and measure MLI2 recruitment and learning.
Image Purkinje dendritic calcium with MLI2s silenced, for errors versus rewards.
Model whether synchrony-gated plasticity explains learning-rate differences across microzones.

questions.title: What drives non-motor cerebellar behaviors?
questions.text: Silencing granule-cell signaling spares social preference and anxiety, but silencing Purkinje output does not. Are these behaviors driven by intrinsic Purkinje firing, climbing fibers, or downstream compensation?
approaches: Silence climbing fibers or granule cells acutely in adults versus during development.
Clamp Purkinje firing patterns optogenetically while social behavior is tested.
Trace downstream compensation after early cerebellar lesions with whole-brain imaging.

questions.title: Is the cerebellum a cognitive reserve?
questions.text: Larger cerebellar volume predicts preserved cognition in aging and in early Alzheimer's disease. Is that causal compensation through cerebro-cerebellar loops, or a marker of overall brain health?
approaches: Track cerebellar–cortical connectivity longitudinally as amyloid accumulates.
Test whether cerebellar TMS improves cognition more in people with low amyloid burden.
Compare cerebellar lesions acquired before versus after cortical pathology.

vestib.label: Vestibular and oculomotor signs (not lesion-mapped here)

flatmap.note: Schematic flatmap in the style of SUIT (Diedrichsen & Zotow 2015). Scores (0–3) are qualitative summaries of the cited meta-analyses, connectivity maps and lesion studies, drafted with AI assistance; check them against the sources. King et al. (2019) found that functional boundaries do not follow lobular borders, so treat lobules as approximate addresses.

circuits.name: Cerebro-cerebellar loops
circuits.desc: Cortex → pons (crossing) → cerebellar cortex → nuclei → thalamus → back to the same cortical areas. Left cortex loops with the right cerebellum.

circuits.name: Olivo-cerebellar module
circuits.desc: Climbing fibers from the opposite inferior olive, Purkinje output to the nuclei, and inhibitory feedback from the nuclei to the olive.

circuits.name: Basal ganglia link
circuits.desc: Dentate → thalamus → striatum, cerebellar nuclei → substantia nigra dopamine neurons, and subthalamic nucleus → pons → cerebellar cortex.

circuits.name: Reward & social (VTA)
circuits.desc: Cerebellar nuclei excite VTA dopamine circuits and reach medial prefrontal cortex through thalamus.

circuits.name: Fear & anxiety
circuits.desc: Fastigial → ventrolateral PAG controls fear memory; fastigial → parafascicular thalamus modulates anxiety (relay to amygdala proposed); dentate → amygdala relieves anxiety after exercise.

circuits.name: Navigation (hippocampus)
circuits.desc: Restricted cerebellar regions reach dorsal hippocampus multisynaptically and synchronize at 6–12 Hz.

circuits.name: Satiation (gut → DCN)
circuits.desc: Gut nutrients activate anterior DCN neurons, which end meals by raising striatal dopamine. Dashed: routes unknown.

circuits.name: Eyes & balance
circuits.desc: Vestibulo-ocular reflex and its adaptation: labyrinth → vestibular nuclei → eye muscles, calibrated by the flocculus using retinal-slip errors.

circuits.name: Body: sensing & acting
circuits.desc: Spinocerebellar input and descending output through red nucleus and reticular formation.
